title: A Celebration of the 90s/2000s Crime Film

commenti.body:
Romeo is Bleeding is one of the best from that time. It's my all-time favorite Gary Oldman performance for sure. It's a sexy and stylish neo-noir, with Oldman playing a dirty cop who's getting squeezed by the mafia and really slipping, and simultaneously trying to keep his head above water with the three women in his life. Lena Olin's femme fatale character, Mona Demarkov, is unforgettable: ingenious, sexy, lethal. Roy Scheider and Michael Wincott round out the cast.

I feel like it may not fit your criteria because of the budget consideration, but The Last Boy Scout is, in my opinion, an excellent crime film that exceeds all your other standards. A strong through-line in crime films of this period was wit, and you can't find a funnier 90's crime film. "Shit, we're bein' beat up by the inventor of Scrabble."

I'm also a big fan of King of New York, New Rose Hotel, Scotland PA, Animal Factory, The Indian Runner, The Way of the Gun, Out of Sight, One False Move, Sonatine, and Erik Skjoldbjærg's Insomnia.

I absolutely love the 90s/00s film bro action genre and I have definitely missed it- yet the 2022 movie Bullet Train felt like it was from the same family and I just despised it. It was like you put everything Quentin Tarantino ever did into a blender and the result just wasn't there. I've seen a lot of compliments towards this movie so I guess it has a following but it just wasn't for me.

Also shout out to Johnny 100 Pesos, a chilean early 90s crime movie. It's a pretty minimalistic crime movie (most of it takes place in a single room) but as far as crime movies not from English speaking countries or Asia go, it's probably the best one I've seen.

I felt the exact same way about *Bullet Train*, and I know what the problem was: No wit.

It WANTS to be like a bigger budget *Snatch*, with a ton of characters and a few cameos, but it lacks the script. Hollywood just can't write good fucking action scripts anymore. *John Wick* is the best action series in a long while because people mostly keep quiet or just talk business.

I think Ladybug was a funny idea, a kind of zen hitman, but that's about it. That bullshit about Thomas the Tank Engine felt like Hollywood QurikyTM.

Not one word in that script matches "You took the jam outta my fucking donut, Tommy"... or "In the quiet words of the Virgin Mary... Come again?"... or "Boris the Bullet Dodger?/ Why they call him that?/ ...Cause he dodges bullets, Avi."... or "You like dags?"... or- You get my point, I think.

True Romance is the epitome of 90s cool for me: the soundtrack, savvy dialogue, stylish direction. I think it has some of the most iconic cinema moments from that decade too: the Clarence and Drexel fight, the Clifford Worley and Vincenzo Coccotti confrontation. 

Time for a rewatch tonight, methinks.

I think this post is allowed here, and should be!  

I think the crime bro kind of blends into other categories, like '90s movies, or Miramax movies.  It's a vibe, hard to define but you know it when you see it.  My all-time favorite movie is Chungking Express, not what I'd call a crime film (although there's criminals in it), but it has that '90s feel to it.  It feels very Tarantino influenced, even though at the time it was made, only Reservoir Dogs was for sure released (came out same year as Pulp Fiction but earlier).  

I too like to pontificate as to why it disappeared.  I think one reason is that everything goes away eventually, Westerns, porno chic, Bruckheimer movies, etc.  Another is that the film business changed.  These kinda mid budget movies don't cut it theatrically anymore, now you need some giant nine-figure budget tentpole, or maybe a low-budget horror, but the mid budget movie is now relegated to streaming, where it'll debut and get forgotten about in a week.  It's lost in a sea of content now.

I'd like to see theatrically released movies make a comeback, with a bigger variety of genres.  I hold out hope that some of these new guys, like the Daniels, will decide to bring it back since it's what they grew up with.

>I'd like to see theatrically released movies make a comeback

Streaming has fucked up the general public's relationship to theaters and how they consume movies, and until the studios can come up with system that both makes them money and lets people watch movies with least possible hassle, that's just how it is.

Personally, I say direct to streaming movies are pissing in the wind.

Also, what is porno chic?

[Porno chic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Porn) was basically around when Boogie Nights was set.  There was a time when mainstream celebrities talked about seeing hardcore porn, which was released in theaters.  In retrospect, there was no big artistic revolution, they started being released on video and it became a low-budget genre like exploitation movies, slasher films, etc.

I think Black Rain is a pretty much forgotten film and you know Frank White needs a piece of the action so King of New York , and you could really stretch this back to Thief as it set the tone for so many much and Mann continued to nail it at the tail end of your list with Collateral.  Also, I'd say Running Scared was Paul Walker at his best.

I wonder how you feel about a film that predates these but also seems to be a kind of forerunner of the genre which is Seijun Suzuki’s “Youth of the Beast” (1963), which tells the now many-times-repeated tale of an outsider who makes his way into a critical figure in a gang rivalry. It is effected with style, panache, and fits of violence. The main echos a kind of Bond-esque cool while also sticking to the grit that a criminal antihero requires.

Interesting topic, I also love this genre

I always thought “Go” was the best Tarantino rip off. Related, “Mr and Mrs Smith” could be considered a rom com version (interestingly 2005)

Not listed above, “Better Luck Tomorrow” is in this vein and worth watching
